deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the draft of §13 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, printed 1867). The question is whether a function f that is integrable only in the improper sense near x=0 must have Fourier coefficients tending to 0. The previous page sets ∫f dx = φ(x)cos ψ(x), with φ→0 and ψ→+∞ as x→0+. So f = φ'cos ψ − φψ' sin ψ. The previous page then applies stationary phase to the term −½∫φψ' sin(ψ+n(x−a))dx. The stationary point α is given by ψ'(α)+n=0. Expanding y = β + ψ''(α)(x−α)²/2 with β = ψ(α)+n(α−a), and using ∫_0^∞ sin(y+β)y^{-1/2}dy = √π sin(β+π/4), the local contribution is −√π sin(β+π/4)·φ(α)ψ'(α)/√(2ψ''(α)).

This page:

(1) Conclusion of the asymptotics. If φ(α)ψ'(α)/√(2ψ''(α)) does not become infinitely small, then the ratio of ∫f(x)cos n(x−a)dx to the stationary-phase expression tends to 1 as n→∞. In the printed text the omitted word is 'Ausdruck'. Implicitly, all other contributions (the other three integrals and the non-stationary parts) are of lower order. This is asserted, not proved.

(2) Power-law case. Suppose φ(x) ~ x^ν and ψ'(x) ~ x^{-μ-1} as x→0. Then ν>0 (so φ→0) and μ≥0 (so ψ→∞). It follows that ψ'' ~ x^{-μ-2}. [Mine:] φψ'/√ψ'' ~ x^{ν−μ−1+(μ+2)/2} = x^{ν−μ/2}. Riemann writes 'of the same order as α^{ν−μ/2}'; a struck continuation of the exponent is illegible. Since α→0 as n→∞ (α ~ n^{-1/(μ+1)}), the amplitude is not infinitely small exactly when μ ≥ 2ν. [Mine:] In terms of n the amplitude is n^{(μ−2ν)/(2(μ+1))}. The previous-page example is ψ=1/x, μ=1, giving n^{(1−2ν)/4}. That matches the earlier claim, with the constant φψ'/√(2ψ'') = ½α^{ν−1/2}.

(3) Interpretation. In the improper integral ∫_x f dx, the increments as x↓0 cancel because of the rapid sign changes of f, although f itself grows rapidly. Multiplying by cos n(x−a) makes the increments near the stationary point add up instead. That is a resonance of the phases.

(4) General criterion (printed version: 'Allgemein wird man finden'). Suppose xψ'(x) → ∞ as x→0, equivalently (Riemann says 'identical') ψ(x)/log x → ∞. Then φ can always be chosen so that φ→0 while φ(x)ψ'(x)/√(2ψ''(x)) → ∞. Riemann rewrites the amplitude as φ/√(2 d(1/ψ')/dx) and then, at the level of orders, as φ/√(2/(xψ')). [Mine:] Since d(1/ψ')/dx = −ψ''/ψ'², we have ψ'/√ψ'' = ±1/√|d(1/ψ')/dx|. For regularly varying ψ', |d(1/ψ')/dx| is of the order of 1/(x|ψ'|). So the amplitude is of the order φ·√(x|ψ'|). Because x|ψ'|→∞, one can take φ→0 slowly enough, e.g. φ = (x|ψ'|)^{-1/4}, so that the amplitude still →∞. Then ∫_x f dx converges up to x=0 (since φcosψ→0), while ∫_0^{2π} f(x)cos n(x−a)dx does not tend to 0.

(5) Final paragraph (partly struck). Two consequences follow:
- Despite the everywhere-possible (improper) integration of f, the Fourier series need not converge, and even its terms may become infinitely large.
- Conversely, despite the impossibility of integrating f on any interval, infinitely many points in every interval may exist where the series converges.

The second claim leads into the next page's examples: Σ(nx)/n, and Σc_n cos n²x, Σc_n sin n²x with Gauss sums. The isolated '…/n' at the bottom is a stray jotting.
errors: Sign of ψ': with ψ→+∞ as x↓0, ψ' is negative and ψ''>0. Hence d(1/ψ')/dx = −ψ''/ψ'² is negative, and the expression φ/√(2 d(1/ψ')/dx) must be read in absolute value (or with −1/ψ').
Replacing d(1/ψ')/dx by lim 1/(xψ') is only an order-of-magnitude equivalence. It is valid for power-like (regularly varying) ψ', not for arbitrary ψ.

'xψ'(x)→∞' and 'ψ(x)/log x→∞' are called identical. L'Hôpital gives only one direction (xψ'→∞ ⇒ ψ/|log x|→∞); the converse needs a regularity assumption. The sign convention (log x<0) is also glossed over.
The claim that the remaining three integrals and the non-stationary parts are of lower order is asserted without proof. It is plausible under the stated smoothness and monotonicity assumptions.

results.what: Stationary-phase asymptotics of Fourier coefficients of f=(φ cos ψ)' and the order α^{ν−μ/2} of the main term for power-law φ, ψ'
results.usually_credited_to: Stokes (1856), Kelvin (1887); Riemann's use in the Habilitationsschrift (1854, publ. 1867) is recognized

results.what: An improperly Riemann-integrable (not absolutely integrable) function whose Fourier coefficients do not tend to zero, even become unbounded, e.g. f=(x^ν cos(1/x))' with ν<1/2
results.modern_name: failure of the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for improper (non-absolutely convergent) integrals

results.what: General criterion: if xψ'(x)→∞, φ can be chosen so that ∫f converges improperly but the Fourier coefficients do not vanish

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of §13 of Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift, matching the printed text almost word for word; the content is well known as his.

checkable.asserts: φψ'/√ψ'' has order x^{ν−μ/2} when φ~x^ν, ψ'~x^{-μ-1} (should give 0).
For the example ψ=1/x the amplitude is ½x^{ν−1/2}; with α=n^{-1/2} this gives ½n^{(1−2ν)/4} (should give 0).
d(1/ψ')/dx = −ψ''/ψ'², with p standing for ψ' (should give 0).
f = φ'cosψ − φψ' sinψ for φ=x^ν, ψ=1/x.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: the struck/garbled condition should read in substance 'wenn [φα ψ'α/√(2ψ''α)] nicht unendlich klein wird' (printed text).
'zu dem [-...-] {+...+}' should read 'zu dem Ausdrucke' (the stationary-phase term −√π sin(β+π/4)φαψ'α/√(2ψ''α)).
The exponent reads α^{ν−μ/2}; the remainder after it is struck.
'[-Im-] Allgemein [?] xψ'x mit ...' is a struck false start. The general statement is the later paragraph, beginning 'Ebenso' (printed: 'Allgemein wird man finden').
'∫_x f x dx' denotes the integral of f with lower limit x (taken up to x=0).
In the displayed formula the intermediate expression is φ(x)/√(2 d(1/ψ'(x))/dx), then φ(x)/√(2·lim 1/(xψ'(x))).
'ψ x / log x' is correct, introduced as 'oder, was damit identisch ist'.
The final isolated '$\frac{\varphi(x)}{n}$' is a doubtful stray jotting; possibly ψ(x)/n or similar.
